note: The Create page example ideas, answered ahead of time. Recorded by scripts/record-example-ideas.js; see engine/example-ideas.js.

examples.idea: I want my class to laugh together

params.aiTopic: silly, absurd, drawable scenes that make a whole class laugh together, like a penguin trying to parallel park or a grandma kayaking through a supermarket

match.explanation: Doodle Bluff has students draw silly phrases, invent fake titles for each other's drawings, and vote on the real one, so the laughs come from the class's own bad drawings and bluffs.

alternates.why: Students write funny captions or responses to a prompt, the class sees them all, and everyone votes for the funniest one, which makes for a shared laugh at the reveal.
Sentences pass through six hands, one word at a time, so the final lines come out absurd and nobody knows what their classmates wrote until the end.

match.title: Doodle Bluff: Class Laughs

params.question: Before lunch, how are you feeling?

match.explanation: A single multiple-choice question students answer quickly, with the results shown as a bar chart, which fits a fast before-lunch check.

alternates.why: The same single question, but the bar chart grows on the projector as answers arrive, with no timer and no waiting for the class.

match.title: Class Poll: Before Lunch Check

examples.idea: Turn everyone's ideas into one class answer

params.prompt: Turn everyone's ideas into one class answer.
params.mergeInstruction: Combine your answers into one stronger answer.

match.explanation: Snowball has everyone answer alone first, then pairs merge their answers into one stronger answer that the whole class sees, which turns many individual ideas into a single shared answer.

alternates.why: Students answer an open question and the projector shows every answer unedited, but nothing gets merged into one answer.
Responses are grouped into themes by AI, which summarizes the ideas rather than building one answer the class writes together.

match.title: Snowball: Turn everyone's ideas into one class answer

examples.idea: Honest anonymous feedback about how class is going

params.question: How is this class going for you so far? What's working, and what would make it better? Your answers are anonymous to the class.

match.explanation: Anonymous Feedback collects honest responses from students, groups them into themes for you privately first, then shares a group-level summary with the class without showing any individual answers.

alternates.why: A quick multiple-choice check on how students feel about class, with results as a bar chart, but it gives you no written reasons behind the answers.
A short, private end-of-class question like 'what's one thing that would help you learn better?', useful for a regular check-in but without the theme grouping.

match.title: Anonymous Feedback: How Class Is Going

examples.idea: Students write encouragement for a classmate

params.notePrompt: One thing you're working on, wrestling with, or quietly proud of this week. Small is fine. One sentence.

match.explanation: Each student shares one small real thing they're working on, then a classmate they didn't pick writes back one line of genuine encouragement, and you review every line before the wall goes up.

alternates.why: Students answer one open question and every answer goes up unedited, so the encouragement would be more about the topic than about each other.

match.title: Someone's Got You

examples.idea: A bluffing game where students invent fake answers

questions.question: What facts should students bluff about?
questions.label: The facts
questions.placeholder: Paste them, or name a topic

questions.question: The Roman emperor Augustus prohibited serving legionaries from ___, a decree that stayed in force for two centuries.
Because of their size, the males of the African driver ant are called "___".
In 1885 the German writer Heinrich Böhnke-Reich warned against using old ___ as coffee filters.

match.explanation: Trivia Bluff shows a real fact with a blank, students write believable fake answers, and the class votes for the truth among the fakes, scoring points for spotting the truth and for fooling classmates.

alternates.why: Students bluff by inventing fake titles for drawings instead of fake facts, so the fun is visual rather than verbal.

match.title: Trivia Bluff

examples.idea: Help my students get to know each other

questions.question: Should students mingle alone, or work in small groups?
questions.label: Alone or groups

tier1Prompts: Window seat or aisle seat, and why?
If our class had a mascot, what should it be?
If you could teleport to any place for just one hour, where would you go?
tier2Prompts: What's something you've changed your mind about in the last year?
What do you think makes someone a good friend?
What's a compliment you received that you still remember?
tier3Prompts: What's something you're proud of that you rarely get to talk about?
If you could thank one person right now, who would it be and for what?
What's a moment from this year you want to remember in ten years?

match.explanation: Closer pairs students to answer the same questions with a new partner each tier, moving from playful warm-ups to more personal reflection, which is built for getting to know classmates.

alternates.why: You would pose one open question and see everyone's typed answers on the projector, a lighter but whole-class version of getting acquainted.
Students draw and bluff each other's silly phrases, which breaks the ice through laughter instead of conversation.

match.title: Closer: Getting to Know Each Other
